A Consistent Set of Empirical Scaling Relations for Spiral Galaxies: The (vmax,MDM)(v_{\rm max},\,M_{\rm DM})–(σ0,MBH,ϕ)(\sigma_{0},\,M_{\rm BH},\,\phi) Relations

Benjamin L. Davis Affiliation: Centre for Astrophysics and Supercomputing, Swinburne University of Technology, Hawthorn, Victoria 3122, Australia Corresponding author: Benjamin L. Davis    Alister W. Graham Affiliation: Centre for Astrophysics and Supercomputing, Swinburne University of Technology, Hawthorn, Victoria 3122, Australia    Françoise Combes Affiliation: Observatoire de Paris, LERMA, CNRS, PSL Université, Sorbonne Université, F-75014 Paris, France Affiliation: Collège de France, 11 Place Marcelin Berthelot, F-75005 Paris, France
2019 May 24, ApJ, 877, 64
Abstract

Using the latest sample of 48 spiral galaxies having a directly measured supermassive black hole mass, MBHM_{\text{BH}}, we determine how the maximum disk rotational velocity, vmaxv_{\text{max}} (and the implied dark matter halo mass, MDMM_{\text{DM}}), correlates with the (i) black hole mass, (ii) central velocity dispersion, σ0\sigma_{0}, and (iii) spiral-arm pitch angle, ϕ\phi. We find that MBH∝vmax10.62±1.37∝MDM4.35±0.66M_{\text{BH}}\propto v_{\text{max}}^{10.62\pm 1.37}\propto M_{\text{DM}}^{4.35\pm 0.66}, significantly steeper than previously reported, and with a total root mean square scatter (0.580.58 dex) similar to that about the MBHM_{\text{BH}}–σ0\sigma_{0} relation for spiral galaxies—in stark disagreement with claims that MBHM_{\text{BH}} does not correlate with disks. Moreover, this MBHM_{\text{BH}}–vmaxv_{\text{max}} relation is consistent with the unification of the Tully–Fisher relation (involving the total stellar mass, M∗,totM_{\rm*,tot}) and the steep MBH∝M∗,tot3.05±0.53M_{\rm BH}\propto M_{\rm*,tot}^{3.05\pm 0.53} relation observed in spiral galaxies. We also find that σ0∝vmax1.55±0.25∝MDM0.63±0.11\sigma_{0}\propto v_{\text{max}}^{1.55\pm 0.25}\propto M_{\text{DM}}^{0.63\pm 0.11}, consistent with past studies connecting stellar bulges (with σ0≳100​km s−1\sigma_{0}\gtrsim 100\,\text{km\,s}^{-1}), dark matter halos, and a nonconstant vmax/σ0v_{\text{max}}/\sigma_{0} ratio. Finally, we report that tan⁡|ϕ|∝(−1.18±0.19)​log⁡vmax∝(−0.48±0.09)​log⁡MDM\tan|\phi|\propto(-1.18\pm 0.19)\log{v_{\text{max}}}\propto(-0.48\pm 0.09)\log M_{\text{DM}}, providing a novel formulation between the geometry (i.e., the logarithmic spiral-arm pitch angle) and kinematics of spiral galaxy disks. While the vmaxv_{\text{max}}–ϕ\phi relation may facilitate distance estimations to face-on spiral galaxies through the Tully–Fisher relation and using ϕ\phi as a proxy for vmaxv_{\text{max}}, the MDMM_{\text{DM}}–ϕ\phi relation provides a path for determining dark matter halo masses from imaging data alone. Furthermore, based on a spiral galaxy sample size that is double the size used previously, the self-consistent relations presented here provide dramatically revised constraints for theory and simulations.

Keywords: 
black hole physics – dark matter – galaxies: evolution – galaxies: fundamental parameters – galaxies: spiral – galaxies: structure

I Introduction

Building on the possibility of unseen mass in the solar neighborhood [158, 164, 200, 239], dark matter has been considered by many astronomers to be prevalent in galaxy clusters since the 1930s [355, 308, 356, 281, 261]. In addition, the study of galaxy rotation curves provided strong evidence for the existence of dark matter [21, 240, 116, 264, 258, 254, 265, 262, 183, 263, 51, 244, 53]. The notion of nonbaryonic dark matter subsequently grew as a mechanism to explain this anomalous gravitational phenomenon [125, 216, 75, 311]. Intriguingly, dark matter is believed to account for 84%±1%84\%\pm 1\% of the total mass in the universe [247], but it remains elusive despite considerable efforts to achieve direct instrumental detection of its theorized particles [313, 5, 10, e.g.,].11 1 See Seigar [283], Arcadi et al. [12], Hooper [152], and Salucci [272] for reviews on searches for dark matter. The concept of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) lurking in the center of galaxies has also had an interesting history of study [see 179, 207, 208, 111, for reviews on SMBHs]. It was in a spiral galaxy, our Milky Way, where an SMBH (Sagittarius A*) was first calculated to exist [212, 273]. For half a century, confidence in its existence gradually increased from suggestion to certainty (see Alexander 7 and Genzel et al. 123 for reviews on Sagittarius A*), with modern measurements [136, 137, 9] even detecting the effects of general relativity [102, 280, 172, 24] in its vicinity, and providing direct imaging via very long baseline interferometry [155].22 2 See also the revolutionary imaging of the central SMBH in M87 [107]. In contrast to dark matter, SMBHs residing at the centers of galaxies are thought to constitute a tiny fraction of the universe’s total mass [131, 334, 84, 232].

Astronomers have long been comfortable with the idea that SMBH masses (MBHM_{\rm BH}) should correlate with properties of their host galactic bulges, as evidenced by a vast literature dedicated to the study of correlations with a bulge’s stellar velocity dispersion (σ0\sigma_{0}), (baryonic and total) mass, stellar luminosity, Sérsic index, etc. [see 129, for a review], although many theoretical models advocate that the total gravitational mass of a galaxy or its most dominant component, the mass of its dark matter halo (MDMM_{\rm DM}), should dictate the formation of SMBHs [206, 142, 306, 63, 141, 225, 4, e.g.,]. The rotation curve informs us about the total mass of a disk galaxy and its dark matter component. Therefore, the rotational velocity profile of a galaxy disk, vrot​(R)v_{\rm rot}(R), can be considered a surrogate33 3 Globular clusters have also been shown to be apropos tracers of the dark matter halo mass; both the globular cluster system mass [309] and the number of globular clusters [57] of a galaxy are directly proportional to its dark matter halo mass. for its MDMM_{\rm DM}. Thus, a relation between MBHM_{\rm BH} and some measure of vrot​(R)v_{\rm rot}(R) or MDMM_{\rm DM} should be expected in observational data.

Recently, we showed in Davis et al. [81] that a significant correlation exists between the total stellar mass (M∗,totM_{\rm*,tot}) of a spiral galaxy and the mass of its central black hole. When combined with the well-known Tully & Fisher [326] relation between the total stellar luminosity/mass of a galaxy and its rotational velocity, one obtains a relation between vrotv_{\rm rot} and MBHM_{\rm BH}. A contemporary study by Tiley et al. [316] has defined the z≈0z\approx 0 Tully–Fisher relation between M∗,totM_{\rm*,tot} and vrotv_{\rm rot} for late-type galaxies44 4 If we calculate the Tully–Fisher relation from our dataset, we find that M∗,tot∝vrot3.94±1.01M_{\rm*,tot}\propto v_{\rm rot}^{3.94\pm 1.01}, which is consistent with Equation (1) at the level of 0.05​σ0.05\,\sigma. to be such that

M∗,tot∝vrot4.0±0.1.M_{\rm*,tot}\propto v_{\rm rot}^{4.0\pm 0.1}. (1)

In Davis et al. [81], we found that

MBH∝M∗,tot3.05±0.53M_{\rm BH}\propto M_{\rm*,tot}^{3.05\pm 0.53} (2)

for spiral galaxies. Therefore, we should expect to find

MBH∝vrot12.2±2.1,M_{\rm BH}\propto v_{\rm rot}^{12.2\pm 2.1}, (3)

which can subsequently be converted into an MBHM_{\rm BH}–MDMM_{\rm DM} relation using an expression from Katz et al. [166] between vrotv_{\rm rot} and MDMM_{\rm DM} .

In addition to our focus on black hole mass scaling relations for spiral galaxies in this work, we also investigate scaling relations between vrotv_{\rm rot} (and MDMM_{\rm DM}) with both σ0\sigma_{0} and the logarithmic spiral-arm pitch angle (ϕ\phi). A vrotv_{\rm rot}–σ0\sigma_{0} ratio or relation for disk galaxies was first suggested by Whitmore et al. [345] and Whitmore & Kirshner [344]. They found vrot/σ0∼1.7v_{\rm rot}/\sigma_{0}\sim 1.7 by measuring Hi line widths for local S0 and spiral galaxies. More recently, Cresci et al. [76] found that gas-rich, turbulent, star-forming z∼2z\sim 2 disk galaxies exhibit vrot/σ0∼4.4v_{\rm rot}/\sigma_{0}\sim 4.4.55 5 The dynamics of newly assembled massive objects (DYNAMO) project [138, 139, 25] demonstrated that their more local (z∼0.1z\sim 0.1) sample of galaxies, selected to have high star-formation rates, are analogs of turbulent z≃2z\simeq 2 disk galaxies, with similar vrot/σ0v_{\rm rot}/\sigma_{0} ratios. The vrotv_{\rm rot}–σ0\sigma_{0} relation represents an intriguing connection between the stellar bulge of a galaxy and its dark matter halo, although for spiral galaxies with turbulent disks, σ0\sigma_{0} may trace the stellar disk as much as the bulge. As a result, regular study of the vrotv_{\rm rot}–σ0\sigma_{0} relation has persisted for 40 yr. We contribute to this legacy with our refinement of the vrotv_{\rm rot}–σ0\sigma_{0} relation and an original quantification of the MDMM_{\rm DM}–σ0\sigma_{0} relation based on the vrotv_{\rm rot}–MDMM_{\rm DM} expression in Katz et al. [166].

As for the connection with the logarithmic spiral-arm pitch angle, Kennicutt [171] and Kennicutt & Hodge [170] presented an observational study of the shape of spiral arms and showed that the maximum rotational velocity of a galaxy disk, vmaxv_{\rm max}, correlated with the spiral-arm pitch angle. They found a definitive anticorrelation, such that galaxies with higher vmaxv_{\rm max} have lower ϕ\phi, i.e., more tightly wound spiral patterns. Their tantalizing empirical result suggests that the trend of shapes across the spiral sequence of galaxies is partly kinematic in origin. We will use our measured pitch angle values from Davis et al. [83] to quantify this vmaxv_{\rm max}–ϕ\phi (and MDMM_{\rm DM}–ϕ\phi) relation, and compare the scatter with other relations involving ϕ\phi.

In this work, we shall endeavor to determine scaling relations from our (currently) complete sample of spiral galaxies with directly measured black hole masses. In Section II, we describe our compilation of σ0\sigma_{0}, vmaxv_{\rm max}, MBHM_{\rm BH}, and ϕ\phi measurements and detail our conversion of vmaxv_{\rm max} into MDMM_{\rm DM}. Section III provides our regression analyses and discussion for six relations: vrotv_{\rm rot}–σ0\sigma_{0}, MDMM_{\rm DM}–σ0\sigma_{0}, MBHM_{\rm BH}–vrotv_{\rm rot}, MBHM_{\rm BH}–MDMM_{\rm DM}, vrotv_{\rm rot}–ϕ\phi, and MDMM_{\rm DM}–ϕ\phi. Finally, Section IV presents our interpretation of the results and elucidates their significance. All printed uncertainties are 1​σ1\,\sigma (≈68.3%\approx 68.3\%) confidence intervals. All magnitudes are quoted in the Vega system.

II Data

In Davis et al. [83], we compiled a comprehensive sample of 44 galaxies classified as spirals and having directly measured (dynamical)66 6 We include direct, dynamical (not including upper or lower limit) measurements derived from stellar proper motions, stellar dynamics, gas dynamics, or maser emission. We do not include black hole masses estimated via reverberation mapping, which is calibrated to the MBHM_{\rm BH}–σ0\sigma_{0} relation [237, 245, 132, e.g.,]. black hole masses (see Table 1). In Davis et al. [81], Davis et al. [82], we used this sample to determine how the black hole mass of a spiral galaxy scales with its total stellar and bulge stellar masses, respectively. Here, we use the same sample, plus four new galaxies (NGC 613, NGC 1365, NGC 1566, and NGC 1672) from Combes et al. [67], making our total sample of spiral galaxies with directly measured black hole masses twice the size of recent studies [267, e.g.,]. For this expanded sample, we tabulate the ϕ\phi and σ0\sigma_{0} measurements [83, predominantly from], plus the vmaxv_{\rm max} measurements that we have assembled from the literature. We use this rotational velocity to draw a connection to the dark matter halo mass, which dictates the maximum rotational velocity at the outer radii of a galaxy. As revealed in Davis et al. [83], particular care was taken to obtain the fundamental spiral-arm pitch angle rather than the harmonics, which may be a factor of two or three smaller or larger and are accidentally obtained when an insufficiently long section of spiral arms is used.

Forty-two galaxies out of our total sample of 48 galaxies have vmaxv_{\rm max} measurements in the literature. These are mostly (29 out of 42) from the HyperLeda database77 7 http://leda.univ-lyon1.fr/ [243], which provides homogenized maximum rotational velocities calculated from the 21 cm line maximum widths (WmaxW_{\rm max}) or available rotation curves (generally Hα\alpha rotation curves). These velocities are derived from the observed line-of-sight velocities (vobsv_{\rm obs}), after correcting for inclination (ii), such that

vmax=Wmax2​sin⁡(i)=vobssin⁡(i).v_{\rm max}=\frac{W_{\rm max}}{2\sin(i)}=\frac{v_{\rm obs}}{\sin(i)}. (4)

The internal orbital velocity for a galaxy at a given radius can be used to estimate the mass of the galaxy interior to that radius; this mass is the sum of the baryonic and nonbaryonic (i.e., dark matter) masses. At the outer regions of a galaxy, the gravitational potential is thought to be dominated by the dark matter halo (but see Milgrom 224 and McGaugh & Schombert 220), for which the maximum rotational velocity is a proxy.

For our conversions from vmaxv_{\rm max} into MDMM_{\rm DM}, we consulted the recent work of Katz et al. [166], who determined MDMM_{\rm DM}–vrotv_{\rm rot} relations from the Spitzer Photometry and Accurate Rotation Curves (SPARC) sample gas and stellar mass models [196] and employed the Markov chain Monte Carlo simulations from Katz et al. [167] to empirically determine halo masses. [166] present evidence that a variety of rotational measurements are capable of accurately predicting dark matter halo masses in spiral galaxies. They explored many of the standard measurements: (i) vflatv_{\rm flat}, the rotational velocity along the flat portion of a rotation curve, (ii) v2.2v_{2.2}, the rotational velocity at 2.2 disk scale lengths, (iii) veffv_{\rm eff}, the rotational velocity at the effective half-light radius of a galaxy, and (iv) vmaxv_{\rm max}. Katz et al. [166] presented empirical relations for the MDMM_{\rm DM}–vflatv_{\rm flat}, MDMM_{\rm DM}–v2.2v_{2.2}, MDMM_{\rm DM}–veffv_{\rm eff}, and MDMM_{\rm DM}–vmaxv_{\rm max} relations from a sample of 120 late-type galaxies with rotational velocity measurements and dark matter halo masses estimated using the Di Cintio et al. [92] halo profile. Their halo profile model is derived from cosmological galaxy formation simulations, which account for baryonic processes affecting their host dark matter halos [92, 93, 13], unlike cosmological dark matter-only simulations [234].88 8 Katz et al. [166] also compared their results with halo masses derived from the Navarro et al. [234] halo profile, but found poor results owing to “the cusp-core problem” for galaxies with slowly rising rotation curves [88, 87, 122, 185, 184, 186, 167]. Katz et al. [166] argue that tight relations between all of these choices for rotational velocity indicate that the kinematics of a late-type galaxy, at radii much smaller than its virial radius,99 9 Katz et al. [166] note that vflatv_{\rm flat} is generally measured at a radius farther out than the typical measurement radii of v2.2v_{2.2}, veffv_{\rm eff}, or vmaxv_{\rm max}, where the halo influence dominates the rotation curve. Even at the radius (rflatr_{\rm flat}) where vflatv_{\rm flat} is measured, they deduce that ∼93%\sim 93\% (on average) of a halo mass is external to rflatr_{\rm flat}. can be reliably used to estimate its halo mass.

Based on their sample of 120 late-type galaxies, they concluded that all of these different measures produce consistent results. We have elected to use vmaxv_{\rm max} due to its ubiquity in published extragalactic Hi source catalogs. Additionally, we assume that vmaxv_{\rm max} is an accurate tracer of the circular velocity (vcircv_{\rm circ}) for spiral galaxies at large radii (i.e., vcirc≡vmaxv_{\rm circ}\equiv v_{\rm max}). We employ the MDMM_{\rm DM}–vmaxv_{\rm max} relation from Katz et al. [166], which is such that

III Analysis and Discussion

III.1 The vmaxv_{\rm max}–σ0\sigma_{0} Relation

The correlation between vrotv_{\rm rot} and σ0\sigma_{0} suggests a relationship between the dark matter halo and the stellar bulge of a galaxy, at least for galaxies with bulges. Ferrarese [110] initially presented an empirical vrotv_{\rm rot}–σ0\sigma_{0} relation involving 38 spiral galaxies. Baes et al. [22] followed up this work by adding a dozen spiral galaxies and found a consistent, tight correlation. Pizzella et al. [246] then argued that the vrotv_{\rm rot}–σ0\sigma_{0} relation is different for high- and low surface brightness galaxies, while Ho [150, and later ] showed from a large sample of 792 galaxies with diverse morphological types that the vrotv_{\rm rot}–σ0\sigma_{0} relation varies significantly for subsamples based on morphology. Courteau et al. [73] subsequently showed that massive galaxies scattered about a vrot=2​σ0v_{\rm rot}=\sqrt{2}\sigma_{0} relation [see 298, who found vrot=1.33​σ0v_{\rm rot}=1.33\sigma_{0} for early-type galaxies] and pure disks obeyed vrot≃2​σ0v_{\rm rot}\simeq 2\sigma_{0}, and they advocated that a trivariate relationship with total light concentration was needed to properly model the data.

Here, we produce a vmaxv_{\rm max}–σ0\sigma_{0} relation for the 40 spiral galaxies with both vmaxv_{\rm max} and σ0\sigma_{0} measurements (not including NGC 4395). Knowing σ0\sigma_{0}, this relation can be used to estimate vmaxv_{\rm max}, and indirectly predict MDMM_{\rm DM} (through Equation (5)); this is useful for galaxies with velocity dispersion measurements that lack reliable rotational velocity measurements (e.g., nearly face-on disk galaxies). The bces bisector regression [6, 235]1212 12 https://github.com/rsnemmen/BCES yields

log⁡(vmaxkm​s−1)\displaystyle\log\left(\frac{v_{\rm max}}{\rm km\,s^{-1}}\right) =\displaystyle= (0.65±0.10)​log⁡(σ0141​km​s−1)\displaystyle(0.65\pm 0.10)\log\left(\frac{\sigma_{0}}{141\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}}\right) (6)
+(2.34±0.01),\displaystyle+\>(2.34\pm 0.01),

with Δrms=0.08\Delta_{\rm rms}=0.08 dex and intrinsic scatter1313 13 Calculated through Equation (1) from Graham & Driver [130]. ϵ=0.07\epsilon=0.07 dex, both in the log⁡vmax\log v_{\rm max} direction (see Figure 1).

Except for NGC 4395, it is apparent from inspection of Figure 1 that five galaxies (Circinus, NGC 613, NGC 1300, NGC 4151, and NGC 5055) are mild outliers, noticeably outside the ±1​σ\pm 1\,\sigma (±1​Δrms\pm 1\,\Delta_{\rm rms}) scatter band. Of these five galaxies, two galaxies (NGC 1300 and NGC 5055) are >2​σ>2\,\sigma outliers. Davis et al. [81] note that NGC 1300 is an outlier in the MBHM_{\rm BH}–M∗,totM_{\rm*,tot} diagram for spiral galaxies, with either an overmassive black hole or a low total stellar mass, which is matched here by either a low vmaxv_{\rm max} or a high σ0\sigma_{0}. Davis et al. [83] pointed out that NGC 5055 is an outlier in the MBHM_{\rm BH}–σ0\sigma_{0} diagram for spiral galaxies, with either an overmassive black hole or a low central stellar velocity dispersion.

Our (σ0,vmax)(\sigma_{0},\,v_{\rm max}) dataset can be described by a Pearson correlation coefficient r=0.41r=0.41, and a pp-value probability equal to 9.35×10−39.35\times 10^{-3} that the null hypothesis is true. The Spearman rank-order correlation coefficient rs=0.40r_{s}=0.40, with ps=1.07×10−2p_{s}=1.07\times 10^{-2} that the null hypothesis is true. However, the slope of the vmaxv_{\rm max}–σ0\sigma_{0} relation is inconsistent with a value of 1 at the 3.5​σ3.5\,\sigma level. That is, vmax/σ0v_{\rm max}/\sigma_{0} is not a constant ratio. We do, however, acknowledge that the vmaxv_{\rm max}–σ0\sigma_{0} relation may be bent or curved, but we require more data with σ0<100​km​s−1\sigma_{0}<100\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}} to see this. We find that the slope of our vmaxv_{\rm max}–σ0\sigma_{0} relation is shallower than but consistent with the vrotv_{\rm rot}–σ0\sigma_{0} slope (0.84±0.090.84\pm 0.09) from Ferrarese [110] for 38 spiral galaxies; the slope (0.74±0.070.74\pm 0.07) from Pizzella et al. [246] for 40 high surface brightness disk galaxies, eight giant low surface brightness galaxies, and 24 elliptical galaxies; and the slope (0.90±0.150.90\pm 0.15) from Kormendy & Bender [176] for 30 spiral galaxies, which are a subset of the Ferrarese [110] sample; at the levels of 1.00​σ1.00\,\sigma, 0.53​σ0.53\,\sigma, and 1.00​σ1.00\,\sigma, respectively.

Our sample selection of only galaxies with dynamically estimated black hole masses does appear to have resulted in a selection bias, artificially truncating data such that we have a deficit of galaxies with σ0≲100​km​s−1\sigma_{0}\lesssim 100\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}} (as seen in Figure 1). Lynden-Bell et al. [213, their Figure 10] discuss this problem and present a solution by modifying the type of linear regression. By using a regression of log⁡vmax\log v_{\rm max} on log⁡σ0\log\sigma_{0}, i.e., the bces(Y||X) routine that minimizes the residuals in the Y-direction, we can generate a relation that is less strongly affected by this bias. Doing so, we find

log⁡(vmaxkm​s−1)\displaystyle\log\left(\frac{v_{\rm max}}{\rm km\,s^{-1}}\right) =\displaystyle= (0.30±0.11)​log⁡(σ0141​km​s−1)\displaystyle(0.30\pm 0.11)\log\left(\frac{\sigma_{0}}{141\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}}\right) (7)
+(2.33±0.01),\displaystyle+\>(2.33\pm 0.01),

with Δrms=0.07\Delta_{\rm rms}=0.07 dex and ϵ=0.06\epsilon=0.06 dex, both in the log⁡vmax\log v_{\rm max} direction (see Figure 1).

Indeed, it is prudent to show concern for possible selection bias. Batcheldor [26] pointed out that a false MBHM_{\rm BH}–σ0\sigma_{0} relation can be obtained from galaxies with randomly assigned black hole masses by imposing a spatial resolution cutoff to censor unresolvable spheres of influence. Thus, it is important to be cautious about unobserved data in samples of spiral galaxies with dynamical black hole mass estimates. However, it is also possible that the vmaxv_{\rm max}–σ0\sigma_{0} relation breaks down for small galaxies. For example, Courteau et al. [73, see their Figure 1] show that the vmaxv_{\rm max}–σ0\sigma_{0} relation only holds for galaxies with σ0≳80​km​s−1\sigma_{0}\gtrsim 80\,{\rm km\,s}^{-1} and vmax≳200​km​s−1v_{\rm max}\gtrsim 200\,{\rm km\,s}^{-1}, and they attribute the breakdown for smaller galaxies to less certain rotational and dispersion estimates due to amplified gas turbulence, velocity anisotropy, and measurement errors.

III.1.1 Pseudobulges

Galaxies that allegedly contain pseudobulges1414 14 See Fisher & Drory [112] for a review, summarizing the observed properties of pseudobulges and classical bulges, and see Graham [128] for concerns with identifying pseudobulges, splitting what may be a bulge continuum, and galaxies hosting both types of bulge [see 156, for semianalytical models of galaxy formation yielding composite bulges]. Equally concerning, Costantin et al. [71] assess that bulge classification is difficult with any observational diagnostic other than their intrinsic three-dimensional shape; classical bulges appear as thick oblate spheroids, with pseudobulges distinguishable by their relative disk-like flattening. constitute the bulk of our sample [83, i.e., 36 out of 42;]. For local (z∼0z\sim 0) galaxies, the central stellar velocity dispersion is primarily a measurement of the kinematics of the bulge; however, for those galaxies with only pseudobulges or small bulges, the kinematics of the bar and disk will contribute in a higher proportion than the weak contribution in galaxies with large classical bulges [73].1515 15 Similarly, the use of σe\sigma_{e} (the velocity dispersion within the effective half-light radius of a galaxy) is not desirable because it is heavily biased by any bar or disk in the galaxy. Hartmann et al. [146] show that the central σ0\sigma_{0} is not only σ0​(bulge)\sigma_{0}({\rm bulge}) but rather σ0​(bulge+disk)\sigma_{0}({\rm bulge}+{\rm disk}) due to contamination by the disk, which increases with disk inclination. When a classical bulge does not dominate, it is important to take into account the disk, the effect of gas (whereas the gas is negligible in massive galaxies and ellipticals), the bar orientation,1616 16 Bars, when viewed from an end-on orientation, may exhibit a small secondary biasing effect. Sight-lines down the major axis of a bar should elevate the observed σ0\sigma_{0}, and thus more edge-on disks would have higher σ0\sigma_{0} values if the bar were additionally positioned in the right way within the disk plane for this sight-line to occur. the spectral line used for the measurement,1717 17 Harris et al. [144] point out that the spectral line used for the measurement of σ0\sigma_{0} can bias the result by as much as 8%8\%. the rotation,1818 18 Spectroscopic measurements of velocity dispersion through a fixed aperture do not yield reliable estimates for the true σ0\sigma_{0} of a galaxy due to contamination from galactic rotation [314, 41, 332, 147]. Kang et al. [163] address the problem of rotation contaminating the σ0\sigma_{0} measurement and try to remove the rotation and isolate the true σ0\sigma_{0} with small apertures. They report consistent σ0\sigma_{0} values from the optical and near-infrared absorption lines, but find that a rotation component can cause σ0\sigma_{0} to vary by up to ∼20%\sim 20\% in a single-aperture spectrum. and the inclination. These complications are beyond the scope of this project; however, we might suspect a dependency on inclination for our sample, especially for the galaxies with the lowest observed σ0\sigma_{0} values, where disk star contamination (if present) will be fractionally more noteworthy. An additional investigation of the bar strength is beyond the desired scope of this work; however, a significant follow-up study might garner further insight. For example, NGC 613 and NGC 1300 (both classical barred galaxies) are prominent outliers in Figure 1, suggesting that their bars might have significantly altered the kinematics of these galaxies.

Graham et al. [132] demonstrate that the scatter in the MBHM_{\rm BH}–σ0\sigma_{0} diagram can be mitigated by fitting an offset relation for barred galaxies. For pseudobulges built from bars, the “bulge” is very flattened, and the velocity dispersion is anisotropic, much larger in the horizontal direction than in the vertical direction. Bellovary et al. [33] specifically treat this anisotropic issue, and show that increased inclination not only produces an elevated scatter at the low-mass end of the MBHM_{\rm BH}–σ0\sigma_{0} relation, but also introduces a bias, to increase globally both the average and the median value above the true σ0\sigma_{0}, which tends to show an offset MBHM_{\rm BH}–σ0\sigma_{0} relation for disky galaxies. This bias applies not just to barred galaxies but all to spiral galaxies because all spiral galaxies will likely possess a bar at some point in their life. Sheth et al. [300] describe the development of a bar as an indicator of maturity, although bars may be recurrent and therefore not a sign of either maturity or immaturity.

In consideration of the effects of inclination, we have investigated σ0\sigma_{0} vs. sin⁡(i)\sin(i) and found no correlation. We do, however, note that some galaxies have uncharacteristically low σ0\sigma_{0} values. For instance, NGC 253 (the Sculptor galaxy) has σ0=(96±18)​km​s−1\sigma_{0}=(96\pm 18)\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}, but it is a bulgy, massive, and inclined (i=75​.∘​3i=75\fdg 3) galaxy. Perhaps some explanation for this galaxy can be obtained by considering that NGC 253 is a prototypical starburst galaxy [342, 180, 197, 214, 215, 312]. As a result, σ0\sigma_{0} may depend on the age of the stars: when there is gas, young stars can form from the gas, strongly weight the optical spectrum, and ‘‘cool’’ the stellar component.1919 19 This is contrary to a collision-less simulation, where the stellar component only heats up. This process in the disk can contribute to the measurement of σ0\sigma_{0}, leading to a small σ0\sigma_{0}-drop at the center of a galaxy and could explain why σ0\sigma_{0} is low for NGC 253 and other star-forming galaxies. Indeed, other prominent starburst galaxies display this behavior. The vmax/σ0v_{\rm max}/\sigma_{0} ratios of NGC 253 and three other prominent star-forming galaxies, IC 342, NGC 2146, and NGC 6946 [see 127, and references therein], are all elevated with vmax/σ0=2.04±0.38v_{\rm max}/\sigma_{0}=2.04\pm 0.38, 3.11±0.493.11\pm 0.49, 2.33±0.162.33\pm 0.16, and 5.66±0.985.66\pm 0.98 (all from HyperLeda), respectively. Moreover, the bar in NGC 253 is not end-on but inclined (if not completely side-on), reducing its effect on σ0\sigma_{0}.

The widespread presence of low- to medium-luminosity, active galactic nuclei (AGNs) in spiral galaxies [32, 159, 347, e.g.,] indicates that the efficient growth of SMBHs through the accretion of gas is prevalent. It is evident that secular processes in disk galaxies play a key role in the development of SMBHs [65, 279, 278, 11, 173, 307, 321, 90, 354]. Nuclear bars have been theorized to drive gas inflows into the center, feeding black holes [304, 303, 153, e.g.,]. Du et al. [98, see also ] considered the effect of an SMBH on a nuclear bar, showing that nuclear bars are destroyed at lower SMBH masses than the large-scale bars in their simulations. Specifically, they found that embedded bars are quickly dissolved when MBH≳0.2%​M∗,totM_{\rm BH}\gtrsim 0.2\%\,M_{\rm*,tot}, halting the inner-bar-driven gas-feeding mechanism. For comparison, we find that for the subsample of 35 pseudobulge spiral galaxies in Davis et al. [81], the median ratio is is approximately an order of magnitude lower, MBH=(0.016%±0.011%)​M∗,totM_{\rm BH}=(0.016\%\pm 0.011\%)\,M_{\rm*,tot}.

The central velocity dispersion is enhanced by the presence of a bar, ultimately leading to slightly higher values of σ0\sigma_{0} in barred galaxies than in unbarred galaxies. Hartmann et al. [146] conducted simulations, showing that bar growth heats the disk, forms the bulge, and concentrates the mass,2020 20 The bar strength is not necessarily a clear indicator of mass concentration, as a galaxy could have already passed its maturity, concentrated its mass, and its once strong bar could now appear weakened or have disappeared. therefore the mass evolution increases the central velocity dispersion,2121 21 The simulations of Hartmann et al. [146] show that the formation of a bar yields an elevated σ0\sigma_{0} even when viewing the disk face-on. This suggests a connection with out-of-plane buckling that leads to peanut shell-shaped structures [55, 89, 154, 157, 66, 56, 210, 211, 242, 60, 16, 64] that are more readily visible in edge-on spiral galaxies, but are also recognizable in more face-on systems [193, 190, 191, 192, 194, 106, 17, 62, 188, 189, 149, 270, 271, 268]. The bar or peanut shell shape may also increase the vertical dispersion of the disk, in addition to the bar, but this is a small effect considering the great streaming in the disk. Therefore, if Hartmann et al. [146] see an effect for i=0​°i=0\arcdeg, it is more likely due to the concentration of the mass in the center and the global heating than due to the peanut shell shape. Moreover, when gas is present, there is a diminished box or peanut shell-shape effect; the presence of a large gas fraction tends to weaken or destroy the peanut shell shape. which causes barred galaxies to move to higher velocity dispersions in the MBHM_{\rm BH}–σ0\sigma_{0} diagram. However, their simulations did not include gas [297, see], which meant that gas was not present to possibly form new stars (cooling the stellar component and decreasing σ0\sigma_{0}) or fuel SMBHs in their galaxies (increase MBHM_{\rm BH}). From complementary simulations, Brown et al. [54] found that the growth of an SMBH also affects the nuclear stellar kinematics of a galaxy, increasing σ0\sigma_{0}.2222 22 Hartmann et al. [146] remark that the increase in σ0\sigma_{0} due to SMBH growth within a bar, seen by Brown et al. [54], is only a small effect (∼7%\sim 7\%) compared to that resulting from the formation and evolution of a bar.

III.1.2 The MDMM_{\rm DM}–σ0\sigma_{0} Relation

As mentioned in Section I, some theoretical models suggest that dark matter halos should be related to the mass of their SMBHs. Additionally, lambda cold dark matter (Λ\LambdaCDM) disk–bulge–halo models indicate that the disks and bulges are formed from the cooling of baryons inside dark matter halos, implying that the disk and bulge of a galaxy should also be partially determined by the properties of its dark matter halo [142, 330, 353, e.g.,]. As a consequence of this bulge–halo connection and the known MBHM_{\rm BH}–σ0\sigma_{0} relation, there should be an MDMM_{\rm DM}–σ0\sigma_{0} correlation. Combining our vmaxv_{\rm max}–σ0\sigma_{0} relation (Equation (6)) with Equation (5) yields

log⁡(MDMM☉)\displaystyle\log\left(\frac{M_{\rm DM}}{M_{\sun}}\right) =\displaystyle= (1.58±0.29)​log⁡(σ0141​km​s−1)\displaystyle(1.58\pm 0.29)\log\left(\frac{\sigma_{0}}{141\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}}\right) (8)
+(12.03±0.12).\displaystyle+\>(12.03\pm 0.12).

Additional uncertainty is introduced through the propagation of errors2323 23 Error propagation calculations were performed with the python package uncertainties (http://pythonhosted.org/uncertainties/). when Equations (6) and (5) are combined, however, Equation (8) provides a useful method of quickly estimating MDMM_{\rm DM} in spiral galaxies with bulges when only σ0\sigma_{0} measurements are available.

Zahid et al. [351] examine the σ0\sigma_{0}–M∗,totM_{\rm*,tot} relation for massive (M∗,tot≳1010.3​M☉M_{\rm*,tot}\gtrsim 10^{10.3}\,M_{\sun}) quiescent galaxies at z<0.7z<0.7. They find that σ0∝M∗,tot0.3\sigma_{0}\propto M_{\rm*,tot}^{0.3}, which is the same as the scaling relation between the dark matter halo velocity dispersion and halo mass (i.e., σDM∝MDM0.3\sigma_{\rm DM}\propto M_{\rm DM}^{0.3}) obtained by NN-body simulations [108, 248]. We can compare our result by rearranging Equation (8) to show that σ0∝MDM0.63±0.11\sigma_{0}\propto M_{\rm DM}^{0.63\pm 0.11} for late-type galaxies has twice the slope derived by Zahid et al. [351] for early-type galaxies.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time that the relationship between the mass of the dark matter halo and the central stellar velocity dispersion has been derived or presented for spiral galaxies, although we caution against its extrapolation to late-type (≳\gtrsimSc) spiral galaxies with σ0≲100​km​s−1\sigma_{0}\lesssim 100\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}} that potentially are overinfluenced by the disk kinematics. Alternatively, combining Equation (7) with Equation (5) yields

log⁡(MDMM☉)\displaystyle\log\left(\frac{M_{\rm DM}}{M_{\sun}}\right) =\displaystyle= (0.74±0.26)​log⁡(σ0141​km​s−1)\displaystyle(0.74\pm 0.26)\log\left(\frac{\sigma_{0}}{141\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}}\right) (9)
+(12.03±0.12).\displaystyle+\>(12.03\pm 0.12).

III.2 The MBHM_{\rm BH}–vmaxv_{\rm max} Relation

Here, we derive the MBHM_{\rm BH}–vmaxv_{\rm max} scaling relation for the largest sample of spiral galaxies with directly measured black hole masses to date. Our (vmax,MBH)(v_{\rm max},\,M_{\rm BH}) dataset, consisting of 42 galaxies, can be described by r=0.74r=0.74, p=2.24×10−8p=2.24\times 10^{-8}, rs=0.72r_{s}=0.72, and ps=6.70×10−8p_{s}=6.70\times 10^{-8}. The bces bisector regression yields the relation

log⁡(MBHM☉)\displaystyle\log\left(\frac{M_{\rm BH}}{M_{\sun}}\right) =\displaystyle= (10.62±1.37)​log⁡(vmax210​km​s−1)\displaystyle(10.62\pm 1.37)\log\left(\frac{v_{\rm max}}{210\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}}\right) (10)
+(7.22±0.09),\displaystyle+\>(7.22\pm 0.09),

with Δrms=0.58​dex\Delta_{\rm rms}=0.58\,{\rm dex} and ϵ=0.45​dex\epsilon=0.45\,{\rm dex}, both in the log⁡MBH\log M_{\rm BH} direction (see Figure 2). These levels of scatter place the MBHM_{\rm BH}–vmaxv_{\rm max} relation on par with the scatter (Δrms=0.63​dex\Delta_{\rm rms}=0.63\,{\rm dex} and ϵ=0.58​dex\epsilon=0.58\,{\rm dex}) about the MBHM_{\rm BH}–σ0\sigma_{0} relation for spiral galaxies [83].

The slope for the MBHM_{\rm BH}–vmaxv_{\rm max} relation is significantly steeper than the slopes presented in previous works. However, the steep slope is in good agreement with the prediction from Equation (3), consistent at the level of 0.46​σ0.46\,\sigma, which both confirms that our MBHM_{\rm BH}–vmaxv_{\rm max} relation is in agreement with the Tully–Fisher relation and that the MBHM_{\rm BH}–M∗,totM_{\rm*,tot} relation must have the steep slope of ≈3\approx 3 reported by Davis et al. [81].2424 24 For reference, the MBHM_{\rm BH}–(stellar bulge mass) relation for spiral galaxies has a slope of 2.44−0.31+0.352.44_{-0.31}^{+0.35} [82].

We do not find barred galaxies to be offset in our MBHM_{\rm BH}–vmaxv_{\rm max} relation (see Figure 2); the bulk of our galaxies have barred morphologies (35 out of 42). Courteau et al. [72] found that barred galaxies are not offset in the Tully–Fisher relation, reinforcing our finding that vmaxv_{\rm max} appears to predict black hole masses equally well for barred and nonbarred galaxies.2525 25 In a highly influential work, Ostriker & Peebles [241] concluded from their simulations of galaxies that massive halos would act to stabilize disks and suppress bar instabilities; thus, bars would preferentially form in galaxies with low-concentration halos. However, we now know that this is wrong. Bosma [52] remark on the stabilizing influence of a bulge, and Sellwood & Evans [295] find that high central rates of shear can stabilize a disk regardless of the dark matter halo density. In fact, the halo does not stabilize the disk, and even in some cases destabilizes it by increasing the bar instability [14]. That is, a single M∗,totM_{\rm*,tot}–vmaxv_{\rm max} Tully–Fisher relation for spiral galaxies combined with a single MBHM_{\rm BH}–M∗,totM_{\rm*,tot} relation for spiral galaxies yields a single MBHM_{\rm BH}–vmaxv_{\rm max} relation for spiral galaxies.

Based on the behavior of four spiral galaxies, Ferrarese [110] postulated that halos with MDM≲5×1011​M☉M_{\rm DM}\lesssim 5\times 10^{11}\,{M_{\sun}}, i.e., log⁡(MDM/M☉)≲11.70\log(M_{\rm DM}/M_{\sun})\lesssim 11.70, are progressively less efficient or perhaps incapable of forming SMBHs.2626 26 Alternatively, van Wassenhove et al. [333] find that a few percent of their simulated galaxies with massive black holes encounter stripping during their evolution, which leaves them “naked,” having lost most of their surrounding dark matter halos. As can be seen in Figure 2, three of our galaxies (Circinus, NGC 1566, and NGC 4395, two of which were outliers in Figure 1) have log⁡(MDM/M☉)<11.70\log(M_{\rm DM}/M_{\sun})<11.70 (i.e., vmax<159v_{\rm max}<159 km s-1 from Equation (5)). Our results show that 5×1011​M☉5\times 10^{11}\,{M_{\sun}} is not a hard-and-fast threshold; however, given that our uncertainties on log⁡MDM\log M_{\rm DM} are greater than ±0.1\pm 0.1 dex (see Table 1, Column (9)), our smallest dark matter halos are only marginally below this limit. For example, based on vmax=98±7​km​s−1v_{\rm max}=98\pm 7\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}, we predict that NGC 1566 has a quite low log⁡(MDM/M☉)=11.67±0.15\log(M_{\rm DM}/M_{\sun})=11.67\pm 0.15. However, because NGC 1566 is a Type I Seyfert galaxy [8, 236], it is hard to imagine it not possessing an SMBH.

If we track the location of the six outliers from Figure 1 to Figure 2, we find that the locations of NGC 613, NGC 1300, and NGC 4151 suggest that their maximum rotational velocities are anomalous, rather than their central stellar velocity dispersions or black hole masses. Circinus, NGC 4395, and NGC 5055 are not outliers in Figure 2, indicating that they might have abnormal central stellar velocity dispersions, rather than deviant maximum rotational velocities or black hole masses. NGC 4501 is the most significant outlier in Figure 2. It was not an outlier in Figure 1, implying that the black hole might be undermassive, although, it was not an outlier in any of our past black hole mass scaling relations with σ0\sigma_{0}, ϕ\phi, stellar bulge mass, or stellar galaxy mass.

The MBHM_{\rm BH}–vrotv_{\rm rot} relation (and/or the MBHM_{\rm BH}–MDMM_{\rm DM} relation, see §III.2.1) have been studied for nearly two decades [110, 22, 352, 266, 176, 338, 31, 310, 267]. These studies have been conducted on varied galaxy samples, including all manner of morphological types, black hole mass estimates, measures of rotational velocities, and linear regression routines. The published results for the MBHM_{\rm BH}–vrotv_{\rm rot} relations have been quite diverse, ranging from a null result [176] to a shallow slope of MBH∝vrot2.28±0.67M_{\rm BH}\propto v_{\rm rot}^{2.28\pm 0.67} [267] and up to MBH∝vrot7.60±0.40M_{\rm BH}\propto v_{\rm rot}^{7.60\pm 0.40} [338]. None of these results are steep enough to give consistency between the MBHM_{\rm BH}–M∗,totM_{\rm*,tot} (Equation (2)) and Tully–Fisher (Equation (1)) relations for spiral galaxies.

Some of the explanation for why all previous studies seem to have underestimated the slope of the MBHM_{\rm BH}–vrotv_{\rm rot} relation lies in an almost ubiquitous adoption of a nearly linear MBHM_{\rm BH}–M∗,totM_{\rm*,tot} relation. If this were true, then our earlier prediction (Equation (3)) would become MBH∝M∗,tot∝vrot4.0±0.1M_{\rm BH}\propto M_{\rm*,tot}\propto v_{\rm rot}^{4.0\pm 0.1}, which lies in the middle of the findings to date. Such a slope might conceivably make some sense for a population of massive elliptical galaxies that have formed from the result of many mergers, but even then, Sahu et al. [269] find MBH∝M∗,tot1.65±0.11M_{\rm BH}\propto M_{\rm*,tot}^{1.65\pm 0.11} for early-type galaxies as a whole, and, MBH∝M∗,tot1.47±0.18M_{\rm BH}\propto M_{\rm*,tot}^{1.47\pm 0.18} for core-Sérsic early-type galaxies. A linear MBHM_{\rm BH}–M∗,totM_{\rm*,tot} relation is therefore closer to reality for early-type galaxies, stellar orbits are more random, and both kinematical measures, σ0\sigma_{0} and vrotv_{\rm rot}, are well correlated [352, 73, 150] and roughly consistent with vcirc=2​σ0v_{\rm circ}=\sqrt{2}\sigma_{0} for the singular isothermal sphere profile, such that a collision-less system of stars is identical to an isothermal self-gravitating sphere of gas [42]. However, none of this applies to low-mass spiral galaxies, which have been historically underrepresented in black hole mass scaling relations.

One additional factor depressing the slopes of some past studies of the MBHM_{\rm BH}–M∗,totM_{\rm*,tot} and MBHM_{\rm BH}–vrotv_{\rm rot} relations has been the inclusion of early-type galaxies in their samples. Sahu et al. [269] find that early-type galaxies follow a different MBHM_{\rm BH}–M∗,totM_{\rm*,tot} relation than late-type galaxies, with early-type galaxies with disks (ES/S0) exhibiting MBH∝M∗,tot1.94±0.21M_{\rm BH}\propto M_{\rm*,tot}^{1.94\pm 0.21}. Because most early-type galaxies contain disks [104, 181, e.g.,], and lenticular galaxies also follow the Tully–Fisher relation [346], for lenticular galaxies, Equation (3) would become MBH∝vrot7.8±0.9M_{\rm BH}\propto v_{\rm rot}^{7.8\pm 0.9}, a result that is most similar to the results of Sabra et al. [266]2727 27 Sabra et al. [266] obtained MBH∝vrot6.75±0.80M_{\rm BH}\propto v_{\rm rot}^{6.75\pm 0.80} from a sample consisting of approximately half early-type galaxies. Seven years later, Sabra et al. [267] found conflicting results between the relation fit from their data (MBH∝vrot2.28±0.67M_{\rm BH}\propto v_{\rm rot}^{2.28\pm 0.67}) and their prediction (MBH∝vrot5.15M_{\rm BH}\propto v_{\rm rot}^{5.15}) from the observational study of galaxies by Bandara et al. [23]. and Volonteri et al. [338], consistent at the level of 0.62​σ0.62\,\sigma and 0.15​σ0.15\,\sigma, respectively.

III.2.1 The MBHM_{\rm BH}–MDMM_{\rm DM} Relation

Observations find AGN in galaxies with little or no bulge [275, 274] and thus hint at a possible underlying correlation between dark matter mass and black hole mass, rather than between bulge mass and black hole mass [323]. Such observations elevate the possibility of an MBHM_{\rm BH}–MDMM_{\rm DM} relation (with MDMM_{\rm DM} coming from vmaxv_{\rm max} through Equation (5)) in bulgy and bulgeless spiral galaxies, which might indicate that it is the cornerstone of black hole mass scaling relations. However, AGN feedback scenarios [91, e.g.,] suggest that the best correlation should be with the total baryonic mass rather than with the dark matter halo mass (if it is not the bulge mass) because the dark matter halo is mostly outside the baryons, and might not have much effect on the gas inflow to fuel the central SMBH. This means that the MBHM_{\rm BH}–MDMM_{\rm DM} relation would be an indirect result of the MBHM_{\rm BH}–(total baryonic mass) relation.

Theoretical models suggest that the MBHM_{\rm BH}–MDMM_{\rm DM} relation should be nonlinear. Haehnelt et al. [142] demonstrated that the mass function of dark matter haloes could be matched to the z=3z=3 luminosity function for quasars with lifetimes in the range of 10610^{6}–108​yr10^{8}\,{\rm yr}. Their models show a strong correlation between the lifetime of quasars and the slope of the MBHM_{\rm BH}–MDMM_{\rm DM} relation, supporting longer quasar lifetimes as the slope of the MBHM_{\rm BH}–MDMM_{\rm DM} relation becomes progressively steeper; a linear relationship would require quasar lifetimes shorter than 10610^{6} yr. Silk & Rees [306] and Haehnelt et al. [142] posited that MBH∝MDM5/3M_{\rm BH}\propto M_{\rm DM}^{5/3} (here, the typical quasar lifetime is a few times 10710^{7} yr) for an isothermal sphere of cold dark matter, where a proportionality exists between the energy injected by a black hole and the gravitational binding energy (∝G​M2/R\propto GM^{2}/R) of the halo.

Alternatively, Di Matteo et al. [94] suggested that MBH∝MDM4/3M_{\rm BH}\propto M_{\rm DM}^{4/3}, based on their Λ\LambdaCDM cosmological hydrodynamic simulations. Booth & Schaye [50] concluded that MBHM_{\rm BH} is determined primarily by MDMM_{\rm DM} and found agreement with the isothermal prediction of Silk & Rees [306] and Haehnelt et al. [142], with MBH∝MDM1.55±0.05M_{\rm BH}\propto M_{\rm DM}^{1.55\pm 0.05}, which is itself in exact agreement with the observational study of Bandara et al. [23], who find MBH∝MDM1.55±0.31M_{\rm BH}\propto M_{\rm DM}^{1.55\pm 0.31}.2828 28 See also the observational study by Bogdán & Goulding [49], who find MBH∝MDM1.6−0.4+0.6M_{\rm BH}\propto M_{\rm DM}^{1.6_{-0.4}^{+0.6}} from a sample of 3130 elliptical galaxies. However, these results should not be considered applicable to spiral galaxies as these studies focused on massive galaxies, e.g., the sample of Bandara et al. [23] consisted of galaxies with MBH≳108​M☉M_{\rm BH}\gtrsim 10^{8}\,M_{\sun} and MDM≳1013​M☉M_{\rm DM}\gtrsim 10^{13}\,M_{\sun}. Other published slopes for this relation, from galaxies with MBHM_{\rm BH} estimates, include MBH∝MDM1.65–1.82M_{\rm BH}\propto M_{\rm DM}^{\text{1.65--1.82}} [110] for 38 spiral galaxies and MBH∝MDM1.27M_{\rm BH}\propto M_{\rm DM}^{1.27} [22] for 50 spiral galaxies.

Recently, Mutlu-Pakdil et al. [233] found MBH∝MDM1.55±0.02M_{\rm BH}\propto M_{\rm DM}^{1.55\pm 0.02} from a new set of simulations [335], which is in precise agreement with the above findings [23, 50]. Their work is different from previous studies because it focused on extending the relation to lower-mass spiral galaxies. However, their precise agreement with past studies of high-mass galaxies and an isothermal model indicate that their simulations remain tied or tuned to the old black hole mass scaling relations that assume that black holes and their host galaxies follow a nearly linear MBHM_{\rm BH}–M∗,totM_{\rm*,tot} relation. Specifically, Mutlu-Pakdil et al. [233] perceive that MBH∝M∗,tot1.53±0.02M_{\rm BH}\propto M_{\rm*,tot}^{1.53\pm 0.02}, with a slope half as steep as our result for late-type galaxies (Equation (2)), but consistent with the relation MBH∝M∗,tot1.65±0.11M_{\rm BH}\propto M_{\rm*,tot}^{1.65\pm 0.11} for early-type galaxies from Sahu et al. [269].2929 29 From inspection of Figures 7 and 8 from Mutlu-Pakdil et al. [233], we point out an apparent bend in the respective scaling relations with black hole mass. There is a noticeable dichotomy between low- and high-mass black holes, such that it warrants a steeper slope for spiral galaxies hosting low-mass black holes and a shallow slope for early-type galaxies hosting high-mass black holes, rather than their single regression fit to the combined sample. Combining the results of Mutlu-Pakdil et al. [233], MBH∝M∗,tot1.53±0.02∝MDM1.55±0.02M_{\rm BH}\propto M_{\rm*,tot}^{1.53\pm 0.02}\propto M_{\rm DM}^{1.55\pm 0.02}, would suggest that the M∗,totM_{\rm*,tot}–MDMM_{\rm DM} relation is almost exactly linear.

Evolutionary studies show how the M∗,totM_{\rm*,tot}–MDMM_{\rm DM} relation changes with time [143, 29, 30, 28, 228, 226, 227, 195, 348, 251, 341, 43, 209, 257, 182, 230]. Tiley et al. [316] performed an analysis of the Tully–Fisher relation at z≈0z\approx 0 and z≈1z\approx 1 by carefully comparing local and distant samples of late-type galaxies and degrading the quality of the local sample to match that of the distant sample. They concluded that no significant difference is apparent between the two epochs, suggesting an intimate link between stellar mass and dark matter (as traced by vmaxv_{\rm max}) in late-type galaxies over at least an ≈8\approx 8 Gyr period.

The M∗,totM_{\rm*,tot}–MDMM_{\rm DM} relation is traditionally fit with a double power law, exhibiting a steep low-mass slope and a shallow high-mass slope [348, 226].3030 30 However, Behroozi et al. [30] note that a pure double power law is not perfect and results in a MBHM_{\rm BH}–MDMM_{\rm DM} relation that is off by as much as 0.10.1 dex. For the low-mass portion of the double power-law M∗,totM_{\rm*,tot}–MDMM_{\rm DM} relation, Katz et al. [165] speculate that late-type galaxies should follow a theoretical M∗,tot∝MDM5/3M_{\rm*,tot}\propto M_{\rm DM}^{5/3} relation, powered by supernovae feedback and its role in regulating galaxy formation. Furthermore, Katz et al. [165] follow this theoretical prediction up with an observational determination of M∗,tot∝MDM1.51±0.13M_{\rm*,tot}\propto M_{\rm DM}^{1.51\pm 0.13} from their sample of late-type galaxies from the SPARC sample with Di Cintio et al. [92] dark matter halo profiles. Combining this result with Equation (2) necessarily implies that

MBH∝MDM4.61±0.89.M_{\rm BH}\propto M_{\rm DM}^{4.61\pm 0.89}. (11)

Combining our spiral galaxy MBHM_{\rm BH}–vmaxv_{\rm max} relation (Equation (10)) with Equation (5) yields

log⁡(MBHM☉)\displaystyle\log\left(\frac{M_{\rm BH}}{M_{\sun}}\right) =\displaystyle= (4.35±0.66)​log⁡(MDM1012​M☉)\displaystyle(4.35\pm 0.66)\log\left(\frac{M_{\rm DM}}{10^{12}\,{M_{\sun}}}\right) (12)
+(7.22±0.12),\displaystyle+\>(7.22\pm 0.12),

which is consistent with the slope from Equation (11) at the level of 0.17​σ0.17\,\sigma. This slope for spiral galaxies is notably steeper than reported in past studies [142, 306, 110, 22, 23, 50, 49, 233, e.g.,].

III.3 The vmaxv_{\rm max}–ϕ\phi Relation

The maximum rotational velocity does not only correlate with MBHM_{\rm BH} (Figure 2), but it also correlates with, among other things, the spiral-arm pitch angle, ϕ\phi [83, for an introduction, see].3131 31 Logarithmic spirals have been adopted as the natural metric for the form of spiral arms in disk galaxies since the pioneering works of von der Pahlen [339], Groot [140], Reynolds [252], Lindblad [201], Lindblad [202], Lindblad [203], and Danver [78]. Kennicutt [171] observed a correlation between the maximum rotational velocity and the spiral-arm pitch angle, which was later reanalyzed and quantified by Savchenko & Reshetnikov [276]. Kennicutt [171] described the anticorrelation as being ‘‘fairly strong,’’3232 32 Kendall et al. [169], Kendall et al. [168] present a study of ϕ\phi vs. vflatv_{\rm flat} from near-infrared Spitzer Space Telescope imaging and “find no evidence for the strong anticorrelation” that was found in the optical by Kennicutt & Hodge [170]. and claimed that it supports the density-wave theory expectations for spiral-arm geometry [256].3333 33 See the recent reviews on spiral structure in disk galaxies [95] and spiral density wave theory [305] for additional information and historical context.

Our (tan⁡|ϕ|,log⁡vmax)(\tan|\phi|,\,\log v_{\rm max}) dataset of 42 galaxies can be described by r=−0.62r=-0.62, p=1.31×10−5p=1.31\times 10^{-5}, rs=−0.58r_{s}=-0.58, and ps=5.73×10−5p_{s}=5.73\times 10^{-5}. The bces bisector regression yields

III.3.1 The MDMM_{\rm DM}–ϕ\phi Relation

Here, we present new evidence that spiral galaxy geometry becomes a useful indicator for the dark matter content of a galaxy. Combining our updated vmaxv_{\rm max}–ϕ\phi relation (Equation (13)) with the MDMM_{\rm DM}–vmaxv_{\rm max} relation (Equation (5)) yields

log⁡(MDMM☉)\displaystyle\log\left(\frac{M_{\rm DM}}{M_{\sun}}\right) =\displaystyle= (−2.08±0.37)​[tan⁡|ϕ|−tan⁡13​.∘​35]\displaystyle(-2.08\pm 0.37)\left[\tan|\phi|-\tan 13\fdg 35\right] (18)
+(12.03±0.11).\displaystyle+\>(12.03\pm 0.11).

Adding the total rms scatters from Equations (5) and (13) in quadrature yields an implied Δrms≃0.25​dex\Delta_{\rm rms}\simeq 0.25\,{\rm dex} in the log⁡MDM\log M_{\rm DM} direction. This level of scatter is equivalent to that of the M∗,totM_{\rm*,tot}–ϕ\phi relation from Davis et al. [81], indicating a connection between the large gravitational potential well of a galaxy and its spiral-arm geometry, which is manifest in the vmaxv_{\rm max}–ϕ\phi relation (Equation (13)). The ability of ϕ\phi to predict dark matter halo masses in late-type galaxies with such a small slope and level of scatter is remarkable given that no other parameter in this paper is as simple to measure or has such minimal observational requirements.

Mutlu-Pakdil et al. [233] also presented an MDMM_{\rm DM}–ϕ\phi relation by measuring the pitch angles of spiral galaxies produced from the Illustris simulation [335]. They found from 95 simulated spiral galaxies that MDM∝(−0.029±0.001)​|ϕ|M_{\rm DM}\propto(-0.029\pm 0.001)|\phi|. When we fit a linear bces bisector regression between MDMM_{\rm DM} and |ϕ||\phi| for our sample of 42 spiral galaxies, we similarly find MDM∝(−0.028±0.007)​|ϕ|M_{\rm DM}\propto(-0.028\pm 0.007)|\phi|. Therefore, because we find agreement between our observations and the Illustris simulations for the MDMM_{\rm DM}–ϕ\phi relation (Equation (18)), but disagree with Mutlu-Pakdil et al. [233] when it comes to the MBHM_{\rm BH}–MDMM_{\rm DM} relation (Equation (12)), we conclude that the Illustris simulation (and indeed most simulations) fail to properly model black hole mass scaling relations for spiral galaxies. Specifically, the simulations appear to correctly model the total stellar mass of spiral galaxies and the corresponding geometry of their spiral arms but underestimate the mass of SMBHs in spiral galaxies.

The existence of an MDMM_{\rm DM}–ϕ\phi relation (Equation (18)) is not unforeseen; the MDMM_{\rm DM}–ϕ\phi and MBHM_{\rm BH}–ϕ\phi relations can be seen as complementary relations to the MBHM_{\rm BH}–MDMM_{\rm DM} relation (Equation (12)). Moreover, a correlation has been known to exist between rotation curve shear rate (SS)3737 37 Shear is a dimensionless parameter that quantifies the shape (rising, falling, or flat) of rotation curves, and thus is dependent on the total baryonic and dark matter concentrations. S=0.5S=0.5 for a flat rotation curve, S>0.5S>0.5 for a falling rotation curve, and S<0.5S<0.5 for a rising rotation curve [see 288, for a formal definition]. and spiral-arm pitch angle. Block et al. [46] and Seigar et al. [284], Seigar et al. [285], Seigar et al. [286], Seigar et al. [288] have demonstrated the existence of an SS–ϕ\phi relation from observations, and Grand et al. [135] have confirmed the correlation through NN-body simulations. Precisely, S=(0.88±0.08)−(0.014±0.001)​|ϕ|S=(0.88\pm 0.08)-(0.014\pm 0.001)|\phi| [286] and S≃0.85−0.014​|ϕ|S\simeq 0.85-0.014|\phi| [135].3838 38 See also the additional studies of the SS–ϕ\phi relation from simulations [223] and observations [168, 349]. Similarly, Font et al. [114] conducted a comparison of the “shear parameter” (the difference between the pattern speed of the bar and the spiral arms, relative to the angular rate of the outer disk) vs. ϕ\phi in their observational study.

Kalinova et al. [161] introduced a new parameter to classify the rotation curves of galaxies quantitatively: the coefficient of the first eigenvector (PC1) of the reconstructed circular velocity rotation curve of a galaxy through principal component analysis.3939 39 PC1 is a measure of the shape and amplitude of the rotation curve and thus reflects the mass distribution of dark matter in galaxies. Galaxies with PC1>0{}_{1}>0 exhibit high-amplitude centrally-peaked rotation curves and galaxies with PC1<0{}_{1}<0 exhibit low-amplitude slow-rising rotation curves [see 161, for additional information]. Yu & Ho [349] performed an observational study of PC1 vs. |ϕ||\phi| and uncovered a strong correlation (r=−0.66r=-0.66), from which they deduced the implication “that dark matter content might help to shape spiral arms.”

While perhaps not fundamental, ϕ\phi is more a consequence of the presence of a sizeable stabilizing mass, making the disk less self-gravitating. Indeed, when the disk is stable, due to a large central mass (contributed by the bulge and maybe also the dark matter halo), then the pitch angle is small with a tightly wound spiral pattern or even a multi-arm structure. When the disk is unstable, it forms a bar, which can emanate loosely wound spiral arms from its ends. The observational results from Buta et al. [59] support this, showing that the frequency of strong bars progressively increases when moving through the morphological types from lenticular to early- and late-type spirals. Additionally, there can be evolution in time, since violent bar instability heats the disk, which becomes more stable due to a high Toomre parameter, Q≡σv/σcritQ\equiv\sigma_{v}/\sigma_{\rm crit}, where σv\sigma_{v} is the tangential velocity dispersion and σcrit\sigma_{\rm crit} is the critical (i.e., the minimum dispersion needed for stability) velocity dispersion. Toomre [317] established that σcrit∝μ/κ\sigma_{\rm crit}\propto\mu/\kappa, where μ\mu is the disk surface density, and κ\kappa is the epicyclic frequency; κ\kappa is particularly high when there is a high mass concentration, making σcrit\sigma_{\rm crit} small and the disk stable. In the end, what counts is the mass concentration, not only the bulge (which is part of it). Rotational velocity is also a sign of mass concentration; vmaxv_{\rm max} is higher if the mass is more concentrated for the same total mass.

Numerical simulations also illustrate the importance of mass concentration. A sufficient mass concentration in barred galaxies creates two inner Lindblad resonances, inside of which the stable (x2) periodic prograde orbits4040 40 For supplementary reading on families of periodic orbits, see Contopoulos & Papayannopoulos [70], Contopoulos & Grosbol [69], Sellwood & Wilkinson [296], Binney & Tremaine [42], and Sellwood [293]. are perpendicular to the bar and thus do not sustain the bar, but rather weaken it [299]. Mayer & Wadsley [219] showed that bars need a minimum mass to form in galaxies with low surface brightness. Because the disk is diluted and not self-gravitating in a stabilizing halo, this leads to multi-arm or tightly wound spiral patterns with small |ϕ||\phi|. Foyle et al. [115] demonstrated how the mass concentration can change the pattern and also create two exponential disks.

A decade of research has demonstrated a strong correlation between pitch angle and black hole mass [291, 253, 34, 83]. Combining the fact that the geometry of spiral arms is undeniably a consequence of galactic rotation [85, and likely other factors such as the bulge mass and the density of the disk, see] with the results of these aforementioned studies of MDMM_{\rm DM}, MBHM_{\rm BH}, ϕ\phi, and shear, inevitably lead to the conclusion that an MDMM_{\rm DM}–ϕ\phi relation must exist. Notably, the total gravitational mass of a galaxy determines its vrot​(R)v_{\rm rot}(R) profile, shear rate is a parameterization of the differential rotation exhibited by the vrot​(R)v_{\rm rot}(R) profile, which establishes a quasi-static density wave and generates a long-lived logarithmic spiral pattern of enhanced star formation with a unique pitch angle.

Moving farther afield, high-zz spirals are rare but documented in the literature. Labbé et al. [187] presented a sample of half a dozen “large disk-like galaxies at high redshift” (1.4≤z≤3.01.4\leq z\leq 3.0), with some of the nearer galaxies exhibiting “evidence of well-developed grand-design spiral structure.” Contini et al. [68] studied a sample of 28 star-forming galaxies at 0.2<z<1.4,0.2<z<1.4, some of which were identified to exhibit spiral structure. Similarly, Burkert et al. [58] analyzed a sample of 433 (0.76<z<2.60.76<z<2.6) massive star-forming disk galaxies. Recently, Yuan et al. [350] discovered a gravitationally lensed high-redshift spiral galaxy at z=2.54z=2.54 through source-plane reconstruction, making it ‘‘the highest-redshift spiral galaxy observed with the highest spatial resolution and spectroscopic depth to date.’’4141 41 See also the potential evidence for spiral arms in high-redshift submillimeter galaxies from Hodge et al. [151]. Just a few years ago, spiral galaxies were thought not to exist beyond z∼1.8z\sim 1.8, and the spirals found at z≳1z\gtrsim 1 were thought not to be true spirals, merely “spiral-like alignments of star formation clumps” [103]. Studies of these early epochs are essential for evolutionary studies. van Dokkum et al. [331] showed that mass growth in the central regions (and the black holes) of present-day Milky Way-like galaxies occurred primarily between z=2.5z=2.5 and z=1z=1.

The discovery of high-zz spiral galaxies allows for the derivation of the high-zz vmaxv_{\rm max}–ϕ\phi and high-zz vmaxv_{\rm max}–σ0\sigma_{0} relations, which can be compared with their local counterparts, checking for signs of evolution. There may also be implications for the evolution of the black hole mass. Recent results from Drew et al. [97] reveal a star-bursting galaxy at z=1.6z=1.6 with a flat outer rotation curve, which is indicative of a rotation-supported disk galaxy, rich in dark matter and similar to disk galaxies at low redshift. If this single finding is representative of other high-zz galaxies, our MDMM_{\rm DM}–ϕ\phi relation may become a useful tool in the estimation of dark matter at earlier epochs than our local sample. Because logarithmic spirals are scale-invariant curves and are thus unaltered by distance, ϕ\phi might be an ideal messenger to convey an estimate of a host galaxy dark matter mass, especially at high redshifts, if the MDMM_{\rm DM}–ϕ\phi relation does not evolve with zz, and we can therefore use the local MDMM_{\rm DM}–ϕ\phi relation.

IV Conclusions

The vmaxv_{\rm max}–σ0\sigma_{0} relation (§III.1) provides insights into the apparent connection between the kinematics of a galaxy dark matter halo and its stellar bulge. We have shown that the vmaxv_{\rm max}–σ0\sigma_{0} relation, for σ0≳100​km​s−1\sigma_{0}\gtrsim 100\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}, is consistent with studies over nearly the past two decades. We find that the slope is inconsistent with a value of one at the 3.5​σ3.5\,\sigma level, revealing that vmax/σ0v_{\rm max}/\sigma_{0} is not a constant value. We introduce and highlight the implied MDMM_{\rm DM}–σ0\sigma_{0} relation (Equation (8)) and its practical application for galaxies with σ0\sigma_{0} measurements of their bulges, yielding predictions of their dark matter halo masses.

We have presented observational evidence that a strong correlation exists between MBHM_{\rm BH} and vmaxv_{\rm max} for spiral galaxies (Figure 2). The MBHM_{\rm BH}–vmaxv_{\rm max} and MBHM_{\rm BH}–σ0\sigma_{0} relations for spiral galaxies with σ0≳100​km​s−1\sigma_{0}\gtrsim 100\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}} have similar levels of scatter, with Δrms=0.58​dex\Delta_{\rm rms}=0.58\,{\rm dex} and 0.63​dex0.63\,{\rm dex} in log⁡MBH\log M_{\rm BH}, respectively. Alleged pseudobulges dominate our sample of spiral galaxies (36 out of 42). Some may therefore prefer vmaxv_{\rm max}, over σ0\sigma_{0}, as a predictor of black hole masses for spiral galaxies. Our MBHM_{\rm BH}–vmaxv_{\rm max} relation (Equation (10)) is steeper than previous studies, but we argue that past studies did not demonstrate consistency between complementary scaling relations, i.e., the slope we present for the MBHM_{\rm BH}–vmaxv_{\rm max} relation is supported by its agreement with the unification of the Tully–Fisher (M∗,totM_{\rm*,tot}–vmaxv_{\rm max}) relation (Equation (1)) and the MBHM_{\rm BH}–M∗,totM_{\rm*,tot} relation (Equation (2)).

The scatter for the MBHM_{\rm BH}–M∗,totM_{\rm*,tot} relation [81] is higher (Δrms=0.79​dex\Delta_{\rm rms}=0.79\,{\rm dex} in log⁡MBH\log M_{\rm BH}), suggesting that the influence of dark matter, as traced by vmaxv_{\rm max},4242 42 All relations in this work involving MDMM_{\rm DM} are constrained by the Di Cintio et al. [92] halo profile and the empirical MDMM_{\rm DM}–vmaxv_{\rm max} relation (Equation (5)) of Katz et al. [166]. Other relations using vmaxv_{\rm max} are based directly on observational data. (rather than total stellar mass) on the central black hole mass is relevant. The low Δrms\Delta_{\rm rms} value of just 0.430.43 dex in log⁡MBH\log M_{\rm BH} [83] about the shallow slope of the MBHM_{\rm BH}–ϕ\phi relation still remains unmatched for spiral galaxies via ϕ\phi, which is a defining characteristic of spiral galaxies. We acknowledge that these studies [i.e., 83, 81, 82, and this work] focus on a sample constructed from selection of all spiral galaxies with available dynamical mass estimates of their central black holes. Because the sample size (48) is not yet large enough to explore a volume-limited sample, the resulting scaling relations unavoidably suffer from selection effects. Thus, underrepresented populations of galaxies with difficult to measure black hole masses would likely act to increase the scatter in these relations if they could be included (i.e., the quoted scatters should be considered minimum estimates),

Because vmaxv_{\rm max} is a reliable predictor of MDMM_{\rm DM} for late-type galaxies [166], our strong MBHM_{\rm BH}–vmaxv_{\rm max} correlation (r=0.74r=0.74 and rs=0.72r_{s}=0.72) retains its strength when translated into an MBHM_{\rm BH}–MDMM_{\rm DM} relation (Equation (12)). We find steep slopes for these two relations, which is indicative of a history of substantial black hole mass increase through accretion and long-lived quasars [142]. Concerning late-type galaxies, evolution along the steep MBHM_{\rm BH}–M∗,tot3.05±0.53M_{\rm*,tot}^{3.05\pm 0.53} relation implies that galaxies host black holes that underwent rapid mass growth relative to their host (i.e., relative to maintaining a constant MBH/M∗,totM_{\rm BH}/M_{\rm*,tot} ratio). We echo our arguments from Davis et al. [81] that it is crucial to separate galaxies according to morphology when black hole mass scaling relations are investigated. As revealed in Savorgnan et al. [277] and Sahu et al. [269], the MBHM_{\rm BH}–M∗,totM_{\rm*,tot} relation for early-type galaxies is very different.

We have also provided evidence of a link between the geometry of spiral galaxy arms and their dark matter halos. Indeed, the seminal work by Kennicutt [171] qualitatively showed that vmaxv_{\rm max} is well correlated with ϕ\phi, in particular for the later-type spiral galaxies. Such a specific connection between the kinematics of a galaxy and its spiral pattern has important consequences for spiral-arm genesis theories, such as the spiral density-wave (quasi-stationary spiral structure) modal theory [204, 205, 198, 199, 256, 255, 39, 40, 35, 36, 37, 118, 119, 38], swing amplification theory [160, 126, 319, 320, 96], kinematic spiral waves [162, 318], the stochastic self-propagating star formation theory [124, 282], solid-body rotation of material arms [178], recurrent cycles of groove modes [292], manifold theory [260, 337, see also Danby 77]4343 43 Two versions of the manifold theory have been developed: (i) the “flux-tube” version [260, 259, 18, 20, 19, 15] and (ii) the “apocentric manifolds” version [336, 337, 324, 325, 99, 145]; see also the recent work by Efthymiopoulos et al. [100]., superposed transient instabilities [294], etc. We have quantified the vmaxv_{\rm max}–ϕ\phi relation (Equation (13)) to enable and facilitate testing between rival theories of spiral-arm formation [170]. The connection between spiral-arm winding and kinematics can also be applied to the Tully–Fisher relation to indirectly estimate distances to spiral galaxies (Equation (17)). For a complete understanding of galaxy formation and evolutionary processes, it is necessary to study and gain insight into the influence of dark matter. To that end, we have translated the vmaxv_{\rm max}–ϕ\phi relation into an MDMM_{\rm DM}–ϕ\phi relation (Equation (18)) providing for the first time a useful method of predicting dark matter halo masses from the geometry of spiral arms in uncalibrated photometric images of spiral galaxies.

Metaphorically, we can ascribe a dark matter halo as the central nervous system of its host galaxy, filling and connecting all regions of the galaxy. Indeed, the dark matter halo of a spiral galaxy can be considered a legitimate puppet-master, covertly influencing the observable properties and components of its host galaxy. This notion that the dark matter halo determines everything in a spiral galaxy (e.g., vmaxv_{\rm max}, mass concentration, and maybe MBHM_{\rm BH}) has already been put forward by the proponents of modified gravity [224, 221]: when the baryon distribution is known, the implied dark matter distribution and total mass can be deduced.4444 44 From the standpoint of modified Newtonian dynamics, Milgrom [224] would argue that the baryonic mass is the total mass (i.e., there is no dark matter). Much of this dates back to the Tully–Fisher relation [326, 1, 3, 229, 2], refined by the baryonic Tully–Fisher relation [117, 340, 221].4545 45 This critical dependency on the inventory of baryons would also necessitate an accounting of the gas in galaxies as well (i.e., taking gas into account should improve all scaling relations). For our sample, the gas content is thought to be a small fraction of the total mass, and thus we ignore it.

Intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs; 102​M☉≤MBH<105​M☉10^{2}\,M_{\sun}\leq M_{\rm BH}<10^{5}\,M_{\sun}) remain elusive stepping stones in the evolution from stellar mass (MBH<102​M☉M_{\rm BH}<10^{2}\,M_{\sun}) to supermassive (MBH≥105​M☉M_{\rm BH}\geq 10^{5}\,M_{\sun}) black holes (see Mezcua 222 and Koliopanos 174 for reviews). Recent studies [175, 133, 134] have used multiple black hole mass scaling relations, in combination with X-ray observations of nuclear point sources, to identify IMBH candidates in local galaxies. Studies like these provide several independent estimates of black hole masses and serve as important guides for follow-up targets to hopefully confirm IMBH masses through more direct measurements. We offer one additional black hole hole mass scaling relation: MBHM_{\rm BH}–vmaxv_{\rm max}, which, when extrapolated, predicts that galaxies with vmax<130​km​s−1v_{\rm max}<130\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}} (log⁡[MDM/M☉]<11.49\log\left[M_{\rm DM}/M_{\sun}\right]<11.49 through Equation (12)) should harbor IMBHs. For reference, our Galaxy4646 46 The quantity vmaxv_{\rm max} should not be confused with the circular rotation velocity of the disk of our Galaxy at the location of the Sun and equal to (238±15)​km​s−1(238\pm 15)\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}} [44] or (229.0±0.2)​km​s−1(229.0\pm 0.2)\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}} [101]. has vmax=(198±6)​km​s−1v_{\rm max}=\left(198\pm 6\right)\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}} and log⁡(MDM/M☉)=11.86±0.01\log\left(M_{\rm DM}/M_{\sun}\right)=11.86\pm 0.01 [101], with log⁡(MBH/M☉)=6.60±0.02\log\left(M_{\rm BH}/M_{\sun}\right)=6.60\pm 0.02 [48].

Despite claims that MBHM_{\rm BH} does not correlate with disks [177], the MBHM_{\rm BH}–vmaxv_{\rm max} relation for spiral galaxies has similar scatter as the MBHM_{\rm BH}–σ0\sigma_{0} relation for spiral galaxies with σ0≳100​km​s−1\sigma_{0}\gtrsim 100\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}. The steep MBHM_{\rm BH}–vmaxv_{\rm max} relation observed here brings consistency between the Tully–Fisher relation (M∗,tot∝vrot4.0±0.1M_{\rm*,tot}\propto v_{\rm rot}^{4.0\pm 0.1}) and the MBH∝M∗,tot3.05±0.53M_{\rm BH}\propto M_{\rm*,tot}^{3.05\pm 0.53} relation for spiral galaxies. We note that the MBHM_{\rm BH}–vmaxv_{\rm max} relation (Equation (10)) and the vmaxv_{\rm max}–σ0\sigma_{0} relation (Equation (6)) are also compatible with the MBHM_{\rm BH}–σ0\sigma_{0} relation for spiral galaxies [83], i.e., MBH∝vmax10.62±1.37M_{\rm BH}\propto v_{\rm max}^{10.62\pm 1.37} combined with vmaxv_{\rm max}–σ00.65±0.10\sigma_{0}^{0.65\pm 0.10} yields MBH∝σ06.87±1.42M_{\rm BH}\propto\sigma_{0}^{6.87\pm 1.42}, which is consistent with our result for spiral galaxies (MBH∝σ05.65±0.79M_{\rm BH}\propto\sigma_{0}^{5.65\pm 0.79}) from Davis et al. [83] at the level of 0.55​σ0.55\,\sigma. Alternatively, if we cautiously assume that a selection bias is present, censoring galaxies with low σ0\sigma_{0} from our sample, we can instead combine Equation (10) with Equation (7), which yields MBH∝σ03.21±1.19M_{\rm BH}\propto\sigma_{0}^{3.21\pm 1.19}. When we compare this with the (Y||X) regression fit to the MBHM_{\rm BH}–σ0\sigma_{0} relation (which similarly reduces any potential bias due to unobserved galaxies with low velocity dispersions) from Davis et al. [83], MBH∝σ03.88±0.89M_{\rm BH}\propto\sigma_{0}^{3.88\pm 0.89}, there is consistency at the level of 0.32​σ0.32\,\sigma. To conclude, the self-consistent relations presented in this work were derived from a spiral galaxy sample with directly measured SMBH masses that doubles the size of previous samples. These relations necessitate a salient revision to constraints that are applied to theory and simulations.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
